latest_release.name: Python Polars 2.2.0
latest_release.body:
## 🏆 Highlights

- Out-of-core joins (#30679)

## 💥 Breaking changes

- Add Expr.bin.find(\_many), and return char offsets in Expr.str.find(\_many) (#31026)
- Require scalar function arguments at plan time (#30914)
- Make SQL `DELETE` change the registered table in a `SQLContext` (#30869)

## 🚀 Performance improvements

- Parallel streaming cumulative aggregations (#31062)
- Properly assign `Timestamp` unit on ingest (#29699)
- Optimize single-char strip (#31052)
- Add null-equal join support to SQL (#31049)
- Drop the entries of null Map rows without memory per entry (#31014)
- Don't publish join runtime filters to scans too small to skip much (#31025)
- Compare dictionary codes with one code when a single dictionary value matches (#31023)
- Probe ordered streaming joins sync and build one table for small build sides (#31019)
- Avoid redundant dictionary scans and byte-array copies in Parquet writes (#30982)
- Cache plugin symbol lookups (#31013)
- Use the rolling kernels on chunked input in window aggregations (#30472)
- Abandon stalled cloud reads after a stall timeout (#30966)
- Drop unused projections in join (#30740)
- Skip files by predicates on the `include_file_paths` column (#30802)
- Run the SQL lambda resolver through dynamic dispatch (#30930)
- Skip key deduplication when materializing a scalar Map (#30862)
- Don't generate the run reduction for order-dependent reducers (#30929)
- Compare columns through one non-generic function (#30931)
- Skip row groups for `is_in` with an imploded `Series` (#30925)
- Drop unused projections in sort (#30739)
- Store 128-bit group-by keys next to the hash table instead of in it (#30830)
- Reduce runs of consecutive rows of one group as slices in streaming group-by (#30813)
- Skip the hot table for runs of equal dictionary codes in streaming group-by (#30812)
- Keep the probe columns as is in streaming joins on unique build keys (#30807)
- Reduce runs of equal groups locally in sum, mean, min and max (#30808)
- Keep parquet dictionary-encoded String columns as `Column::Dictionary` (#30522)
- Skip repeated values of a group in streaming unique and n\_unique (#30804)
- Handle nulls in horizontal min/max without a per-type option kernel (#30806)
- Reuse the hash table lookup for runs of equal string keys in join probes (#30803)
- Pushdown filters on the `include_file_paths` column (#30785)
- Skip hashing and hot table lookups for runs of equal string keys (#30794)
- Compute rolling\_\*\_by windows outside the generic aggregation (#30795)
- Build dictionaries in casts with u32 or u64 keys (#30790)
- Compute date parts with integer arithmetic (#30777)
- Read IPC buffers through a reader trait object (#30772)
- Rewrite `get(arg_max())` to `max_by` (#30773)
- Gather string views before translating their buffers (#30766)
- Run parallel quantile selection on integer keys (#30761)
- Select quantile order statistics in parallel (#30570)
- Use exact integer ranges of large parquet files for packed keys (#30717)
- Pack multi-column join and group-by keys into fixed-width integers (#30708)
- Compute quantiles and quantile/rank bins by selection instead of sorting (#30569)
- Skip the probe side of joins without non-null build keys (#30692)
- Search sorted numeric slices with branchless binary searches (#30568)
- Optimise decoding of small Parquet `String` and `Binary` columns (#30632)
- Vectorize Decimal mean and sum reductions (#30704)
- Use estimated rows to choose the build side of streaming equi joins (#30681)
- Out-of-core joins (#30679)
- Move inner and semi/anti joins below left joins in more cases (#30694)
- Let null-rejecting string predicates downgrade outer joins (#30693)
- Use column equalities between joined inputs as join keys when reordering joins (#30680)
- Prune unused struct fields in projection pushdown (#30598)
- Implement more fold iterators (#30670)
- Count distinct join keys of in-memory frames for join estimates (#30667)
- Evaluate conditions reading both inputs inside ou

detail.readme:
Documentation: Python - Rust - Node.js - R - SQL | Agents: Skill - MCP | User guide | Discord

## Polars: Extremely fast Query Engine for DataFrames and SQL Polars is an analytical query engine written in Rust. Write your queries with the DataFrame API, in SQL, or mix both: they run through the same optimizer and the same engine. It is designed to be fast, easy to use and expressive. Key features are: - **Fast**: written from the ground up in Rust with multi-threaded, vectorized (SIMD) execution - **Spill to disk**: Operations that exceed available RAM can spill to disk - **Expressive API**: compose complex queries with powerful expressions - **Extensible**: extend Polars natively with custom code through [I/O and Expression plugins](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/plugins/) - **GPU support**: optionally accelerate queries on NVIDIA GPUs - **Interoperable**: uses the [Apache Arrow Columnar Format](https://arrow.apache.org/docs/format/Columnar.html) for zero-copy data sharing To learn more, read the [user guide](https://docs.pola.rs/) or install this [skill](https://github.com/polars-inc/skills/tree/main/polars) in your coding agent. ## Polars in action ### DataFrame API Queries are composed from expressions or SQL. This lazy query gets optimized out of the box and runs in parallel across all available cores: ```python import polars as pl df = ( pl.scan_parquet("orders.parquet") .filter(pl.col("status") == "shipped") .group_by("customer_id") .agg( pl.col("amount").sum().alias("total"), pl.len().alias("n_orders"), ) .sort("total", descending=True) .collect() ) ``` ### SQL ```python import polars as pl df = pl.sql(""" WITH totals AS ( SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total, COUNT(*) AS n_orders FROM read_parquet('orders.parquet') WHERE status = 'shipped' GROUP BY customer_id ) SELECT c.name, t.total, t.n_orders, RANK() OVER (ORDER BY t.total DESC) AS rank FROM totals t JOIN read_parquet('customers.parquet') c USING (customer_id) ORDER BY t.total DESC """).collect() ``` ### Mix both DataFrames and LazyFrames in scope can be queried by name, and the result of a SQL query is a regular `LazyFrame`, so you can switch between SQL and expressions freely: ```python orders = pl.scan_parquet("orders.parquet") df = ( pl.sql("SELECT customer_id, SUM(amount) AS total FROM orders GROUP BY customer_id") .filter(pl.col("total") > 1_000) .collect() ) ``` Read more in the [SQL user guide](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/sql/intro/). ## Performance Polars is very fast. In fact, it is one of the best performing query engines available, for both DataFrame and SQL workloads. See the [PDS-H benchmarks](https://www.pola.rs/benchmarks.html) results. ## Installation ### Python Install the latest Polars version with: ```sh pip install polars ``` See the [User Guide](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/installation/#feature-flags) for more details on optional dependencies
Compile Polars from source If you want a bleeding edge release you should compile Polars from source. Advanced users can also compile for maximum performance for their architecture. This can be done by going through the following steps in sequence: 1. Install the latest [Rust compiler](https://www.rust-lang.org/tools/install) 2. Install [maturin](https://maturin.rs/): `pip install maturin` 3. `cd py-polars` and choose one of the following: - `make build`, slow binary with debug assertions and limited symbols, fast compile times - `make build-debug`, same as `make build`, but with all symbols, produces large binaries - `make build-release`, fast binary without debug assertions, minimal debug symbols, long compile times - `make build-nodebug-release`, same as build-release but without any debug symbols, slightly faster to compile - `make build-debug-release`, same as build-release but with full debug symbols, slightly slower to compile - `make build-dist-release`, fastest binary, extreme compile times By default the binary is compiled with optimizations turned on for a modern CPU. Specify `LTS_CPU=1` with the command if your CPU is older and does not support e.g. AVX2. Note that the Rust crate implementing the Python bindings is called `py-polars` to distinguish from the wrapped Rust crate `polars` itself. However, both the Python package and the Python module are named `polars`, so you can `pip install polars` and `import polars`.
Check the [Installation guide](https://docs.pola.rs/user-guide/installation/) for more advanced installations. For example when you expect more than 2^32 (~4.2 billion) rows, run on an old CPU (e.g. dating from before 2011), or on an `x86-64` build of Python on Apple Silicon under Rosetta. ## Contributing Want to contribute? Read our [contributing guide](https://docs.pola.rs/development/contributing/) and check the issue tracker for accepted issues. Contributors new to the codebase can look for the `good first issue` label to get familiar with the project. You can [join the Polars Discord server](https://discord.gg/4UfP5cfBE7) for any help along the way. ## Distributed Polars Running into hardware limitations executing your queries? Read how you can [horizontally scale your Polars query on a cluster](https://docs.nanook.pola.rs/). ## License Polars is licensed under the [MIT License](LICENSE) (SPDX: `MIT`).
